chapter_theme: How a ruler comes to trust someone: test first and trust only after that, and once trust is settled, don't doubt it. The chapter doesn't expect the flawless. It looks at what predominates, and deeds are its final test.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter by means of knowing: testing by inference (501), reliable testimony (502) and direct observation (503), how to weigh the mixed (504), the instrument (505), then who not to trust, the cost, and the limit of trust (506-510).

501.reading: A person is to be trusted after their nature has been examined through four things: virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life.
501.nuance: My observation: the usual fourth term after virtue, wealth and pleasure is liberation, and here it is fear for life, the most worldly substitute possible. Parimelazhagar defends the wording against a variant, உயிரெச்சம், saying others changed it for not knowing the Sanskrit source.

positions.position: These are four entrapment tests from Sanskrit polity, in which agents tempt the minister with staged plots, wealth, a woman and threats. Passing shows he won't change in future.
positions.quote: உபதை நான்கின் திறத்தான் மனவியல்பு ஆராய்ந்தால் பின்பு தெளியப்படும்.

positions.position: These are qualities to look for: firm in virtue, honest with money, not lost in pleasure and unafraid for his life.

502.reading: Trust lies in one born of good family, free of faults and with a shame that recoils from any blemish.

positions.position: High birth is one of the qualifications in its own right, alongside the others.
He reverses the logic: one who is faultless and ashamed of wrong is the one to be considered high-born.

503.reading: Even in those who have studied the hard books and are flawless, it is rare, when examined, to find no blankness.
503.nuance: வெளிறு is whiteness or emptiness, a striking word for ignorance: a pale spot in a person otherwise solid. Coming right after the demand for faultlessness, this verse admits no one fully passes, which prepares 504. Parimelazhagar takes it as occasional, due to an unsteady mind.

504.reading: Examine the qualities, examine the faults too, examine which of these predominates, and take that.
504.nuance: நாடி three times. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is what makes the verse humane: no one in the world is only good or only bad. Dominance can be either in weight or in number, so this isn't simple counting.

505.reading: For greatness and for smallness alike, one's own deeds are the touchstone.
505.nuance: The ஏ in கருமமே excludes other tests, which sits awkwardly with 502's demand for birth. Parimelazhagar says explicitly that birth, quality and understanding produce the greatness and that deeds are only the final test of it. Manakkudavar turns it into practice: give a small task first, then promote.

506.reading: Beware of trusting those who are cut off: they have no attachments and aren't ashamed of blame.
506.nuance: The logic is that attachment makes a person accountable: without ties there is nothing that shame can work on.

positions.position: அற்றார் are those with no kin. Without them a person lacks the worldly custom that restrains him from blame.
அற்றார் are those without moral conduct.
They are those without principles, not those without kin.

507.reading: To trust the ignorant with fondness as your support brings every kind of folly.
507.nuance: Manakkudavar shows this is an argument, naming Parasara as holding that a king may trust those who love him. The verse refutes that. Parimelazhagar notes the folly is the king's, not only the appointee's.

508.reading: One who trusts an outsider without examining him brings trouble that doesn't end, even down his line.

positions.position: வழிமுறை means descendants: the suffering passes to them, as the kin fall under the enemy.
positions.quote: அத்தெளிவு தன் வழிமுறையினும் நீங்காத துன்பத்தைக் கொடுக்கும்.

positions.position: வழிமுறை means hereditary succession: the error is trusting an outsider as if he were of the ministerial line, and those from such lines may be trusted.
positions.quote: பிறனை ஆராயாதே வழிமுறையென்று தெளிந்தவனுக்கு அத் தெளிவு,

509.reading: Trust no one without examining them; having examined, trust what is to be trusted.
509.nuance: The commentators limit the second half differently. For Parimelazhagar, trust comes for tasks suited to each person's capacity, while Manakkudavar has trust in one matter extend to all matters.

510.reading: Trusting without examining, and doubting one who has been trusted: both bring endless trouble.
510.nuance: The second error is the unusual one. Parimelazhagar's reason is practical: the person senses it and thinks 'this won't last', so he slackens and becomes easy for enemies to detach. Doubt creates the very betrayal it fears.

links.note: 409 ranks the learned low-born over the unlearned high-born. 502 makes good birth the first condition for trust. The two can be squared, but the book's position on birth clearly depends on what is being asked.
349 has rebirth cut only when பற்று is gone. On Parimelazhagar's reading, 506 won't trust anyone without பற்று. The same absence is liberation in Aram and a security risk in Porul.
433 treats one's own millet-sized fault as a palm. 504 takes others on balance, by what predominates. Read together, the Kural sets a different standard for judging oneself and judging others.
972 says standing differs because of deeds, and 505 makes deeds the touchstone. Together they offer a test of worth that doesn't refer to birth, and this is at odds with 502, three verses earlier.
791 says of friendship what 510 says of ministers: examine first, because afterwards there is no way out. Both make trust something with a fixed before and after.

source_issues: 508: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss reads ஆராய்ந்து தெளிந்த where the verse's தேரான் requires 'without examining'. The negative appears to have dropped out, so I did not rely on that clause.
